column2: Can a curve’s rational solutions be read from a related function?
column3: An elliptic curve is an equation whose points can be added together. The manuscript claims the full formula connecting its rational solutions with a related analytic function when a particular algebraic test has value zero or one. The consequence for almost all quadratic twists also uses family 006.

column2: What happens to a curve’s rank as we vary its equation?
column3: Start with any elliptic curve over the rational numbers and vary it by quadratic twisting. The claim is that, in the long run, half have analytic rank zero and half have rank one, with average rank approaching one-half. This is a frequency statement, not a classification of every twist.

column2: Do prime-factor patterns at two different inputs cancel out on average?
column3: Give each integer a plus or minus sign according to whether it has an even or odd number of prime factors, counting repeats. The manuscript claims a quantitative cancellation rule when these signs are compared along two fixed, nonproportional linear patterns. Its broader version has additional conditions on the functions compared.

column2: Can a complicated algebra of arithmetic symmetries be built without hidden relations?
column3: The claim describes a specific algebra of arithmetic symmetries using one basic generator in each odd weight starting at three. “Freely generated” means that these pieces have no extra relations beyond the rules defining a Lie algebra. It is a precise structural statement about that algebra.

column2: Can a field of functions be reconstructed from a smaller algebraic record?
column3: Think of retaining selected arithmetic operations but losing the original field of functions. For fields with at least two independent variables over algebraically closed constants, the manuscript claims this reduced record recovers the field, or a specified enlargement of it. Which recovery is possible depends on the characteristic.

column2: Do certain arithmetic symmetry patterns come from modular forms?
column3: The manuscript links two-dimensional arithmetic symmetry data measured using the prime two to modular forms, a special class of highly structured functions. One result uses a completed space of such data; the classical version needs additional local conditions at two. It does not cover arbitrary symmetry representations.

column2: How large are the prime factors of one less than a prime?
column3: Choose a large prime, subtract one, and factor the result. The claim gives a limiting probability law for the relative logarithmic sizes of all those factors, counting repetitions. A second result says that the function counting coprime residues takes some values extraordinarily many times.

column2: Are the largest prime factors of neighboring integers linked?
column3: Factor an integer and the next integer, then compare their largest prime factors on a logarithmic scale. The manuscript claims these sizes become statistically independent in the long run. In particular, the first integer has the smaller largest factor half the time in the limiting density sense.

column2: Can the prime numbers be made by adding two fixed sets?
column3: Pick two sets of nonnegative integers and take every possible sum of one member from each. The claim says this cannot produce exactly the primes if both sets contain at least two members. Adding or removing finitely many primes does not change the obstruction.

column2: Can two descriptions of arithmetic geometry be matched?
column3: This family claims correspondences between geometric objects and arithmetic symmetry data, plus bounds on associated functions. The geometric claims concern specified groups and curves in positive characteristic. Different parts have different hypotheses, and the Arthur-enhancement result is conditional on a stated decomposition; this is not one unrestricted theorem.

column2: Do arithmetic collections spread evenly through their geometric space?
column3: Certain number fields produce packets of geometric objects. The claim says these packets become uniformly distributed, with no proportion disappearing toward infinity, as the discriminant grows. It covers the particular prime-degree, degree-four and degree-six collections listed in the source, using their prescribed weights.

column2: Can unexpectedly large intersections occur in endlessly many independent ways?
column3: Inside the algebraic spaces studied here, some intersections are larger than their dimensions would ordinarily suggest. The claim limits the maximal exceptional pieces to finitely many in the abelian setting. A companion covers specified curves in a space classifying abelian surfaces, not every possible geometric setting.

column2: Can global symmetry subgroups be described using local information?
column3: The manuscript studies normal subgroups, which stay unchanged when conjugated by any element of the larger group. For the specified algebraic groups over global fields, it claims every noncentral normal subgroup comes from a finite collection of local groups. The local description includes precise openness conditions.

column2: Can the symmetries around a curve identify its rational points?
column3: The claim matches points on certain curves with compatible ways of splitting an arithmetic symmetry group. It covers all smooth proper curves of genus at least two over the stated p-adic fields, and specified modular curves over the rational numbers. It does not assert the rational-field case for every curve.

column2: How often does a polynomial avoid repeated prime factors?
column3: A squarefree integer has no prime factor appearing twice. For irreducible fourth-degree integer polynomials without a fixed prime-square obstruction, the manuscript claims the predicted positive frequency of squarefree outputs. Related results forbid higher repeated powers for other degrees, under the corresponding local conditions.

column2: How long must we search to find a coprime integer?
column3: Fix a number with at most k distinct prime factors. The claim says every block of a constant times k squared consecutive integers contains a number sharing none of those factors. The same constant works regardless of the primes chosen or where the block starts.

column2: How much cancellation remains when cubic Gauss sums are added?
column3: Gauss sums combine many complex numbers whose directions can cancel. The manuscript claims a precise leading total for normalized cubic sums indexed by the specified primes in the Eisenstein integers. It also claims smaller contributions from each fixed nonconstant angular mode; the choice and weighting of primes matter.

column2: How many different answers can the totient function produce?
column3: The totient function counts the residues coprime to an integer. Different inputs can give the same answer. The manuscript claims a precise long-run count of distinct answers below a cutoff, including a fluctuating factor. Multiplying the cutoff by a fixed amount eventually multiplies the count by that same amount.

column2: How few unit fractions can add up to an ordinary fraction?
column3: A unit fraction has numerator one, such as one-third. The claim says every positive fraction below one can be written as a short sum of distinct unit fractions. The worst-case number of terms grows only like the logarithm of the logarithm of the original denominator, up to constants.

column2: Are unusually large gaps between primes genuinely frequent?
column3: Prime gaps grow on a logarithmic reference scale. For any fixed multiple of that scale, the claim says a positive proportion of gaps exceed it throughout sufficiently large initial lists of primes. That proportion can shrink as the chosen multiple increases; it is not one uniform proportion for all thresholds.

column2: Are integral arithmetic points plentiful in spaces of curve representations?
column3: A character variety organizes ways to represent a curve’s symmetries by matrices. The manuscript claims that, after choosing a suitable number field, its integer-valued points are algebraically dense in every component of the determinant-one space. Algebraic density means no proper algebraic subspace contains all of them, not ordinary visual closeness.

column2: Can one fixed number generate all nonzero residues for infinitely many primes?
column3: Repeatedly multiply a chosen integer modulo a prime. Sometimes its powers visit every nonzero residue; then it is a primitive root. The claim says this happens for infinitely many primes for every integer that is neither minus one nor a square, with a quantitative lower bound.

column2: Do elliptic curves over imaginary quadratic fields have modular descriptions?
column3: The manuscript claims that every elliptic curve over every imaginary quadratic number field corresponds to a modular object. The correspondence matches the stated local arithmetic information at every place. It extends the setting of the modularity question, rather than merely calculating examples of curves.

column2: Does a map between arithmetic symmetry groups come from a map of fields?
column3: A field has a group recording the symmetries of its algebraic extensions. For the extensions and continuous open group maps specified here, the claim recovers a unique embedding of fields, running in the opposite direction. The restrictions on the extensions and on the group map remain essential.

column2: Do certain abstract geometric classes come from actual algebraic pieces?
column3: The Hodge question asks whether specified cohomological information can be represented by algebraic subshapes. The manuscript claims this for complex abelian varieties with complex multiplication and for products of projective K3 surfaces. Companion consequences concern other conjectures, but this is not the Hodge conjecture for every variety.

column2: How does a space’s geometric complexity compare with its base and fibers?
column3: Imagine a space organized into fibers over a simpler base. The claim gives lower bounds on the whole space’s algebraic complexity using the complexity of the base, a typical fiber, and how the fibers vary. The results use the particular boundary and geometric hypotheses stated in the manuscripts.

column2: When does a nonnegative geometric class produce an actual map?
column3: Some classes record nonnegative intersection behavior without immediately giving a useful geometric map. Using the stated subadditivity result, this family claims that suitable multiples do give such maps for the log-canonical spaces covered. It also supplies uniform bounds in specified settings; these depend on dimension and boundary data.

column2: Can a mildly singular three-dimensional space produce the expected geometric map?
column3: The manuscript studies a particular canonical class with nonnegative intersections on a three-dimensional algebraic space. When that class has numerical dimension one, it claims a suitable multiple defines a map everywhere. The result requires characteristic greater than three and the stated conditions on singularities and boundary.

column2: Can numerical geometric data lead to simpler models?
column3: One claim says that, under the stated positivity conditions, a canonical class with an extra nonnegative part has the same numerical behavior as a class defining a map. A separate claim supplies minimal models or fiber-space models for specified generalized pairs. Numerical equivalence is weaker than equality of classes.

column2: How much positivity removes every base point from a geometric construction?
column3: Sections of a line bundle may all vanish at some points, preventing them from defining a map there. For a smooth projective complex space of dimension n, the claim says adding at least n plus one copies of an ample line bundle to the canonical bundle removes this obstruction.

column2: How hard is it for a curve to pass through many general points?
column3: A plane curve’s degree limits how many points it can pass through and how many times it can pass through each. The manuscript claims Nagata’s strict bound for at least ten very general complex points. Related results give optimal positivity bounds for sufficiently many general points in higher dimensions.

column2: Can point configurations on certain surfaces be completely measured by one map?
column3: Consider formal combinations of points with total coefficient zero, identified under a relation called rational equivalence. For smooth projective complex surfaces with geometric genus zero, the claim says the Albanese map captures exactly this information. It concerns this special class of surfaces, not all surfaces.

column2: Can a special hyperkähler class produce a fibration?
column3: For the specified hyperkähler spaces, the manuscript claims that a nonzero nonnegative line-bundle class with square zero has a multiple defining a map everywhere. A companion says the base of any projective Lagrangian fibration covered by the theorem must be projective space. The positivity and fibration hypotheses matter.

column2: Do two ways of sorting geometric information agree?
column3: The same moduli problem can be described using Higgs bundles or representations of a curve’s symmetry group. Each description sorts cohomology into layers by a different rule. The claim says these layers match, with the stated index adjustment, in the smooth fixed-determinant setting with coprime rank and degree.

column2: Can two algebraic constructions from a graph encode the same information?
column3: A quiver is a graph with directed edges. It can generate geometric spaces in two different ways. Under the stated stability and free-action conditions, the manuscript claims that the equivariant cohomology of one construction equals the coordinate ring of a specified fixed-point scheme in the other.

column2: Does excluding complex curves force a stronger kind of geometry?
column3: The manuscript considers compact Kähler spaces into which no nonconstant holomorphic map from the complex plane exists. It claims their canonical line bundle is ample, a strong positivity property, and hence that the spaces are projective. Compactness, smoothness and the absence of entire curves are part of the claim.

column2: Does splitting all tangent directions split the whole space?
column3: Suppose a compact Kähler space’s tangent directions divide into two compatible holomorphic families, each integrable into local pieces. The claim says its universal cover then splits as a product in a matching way. For rationally connected projective spaces, a second result supplies the needed integrability automatically.

column2: Can objects on certain three-dimensional algebraic spaces be assigned consistent stability?
column3: A stability condition organizes objects in a derived category by phase and by which objects count as stable. The manuscript claims such a condition with a particular phase symmetry for every smooth complex quintic threefold. It also constructs large-volume stability conditions for the specified threefolds with trivial canonical bundle.

column2: Must repeated geometric flips eventually stop in dimension four?
column3: A flip is a controlled replacement used to simplify an algebraic or complex space. The manuscript claims that every permitted sequence stops for the specified Kähler fourfolds, and that the stated projective minimal-model programs also terminate. The conditions on singularities, rational boundaries and auxiliary data restrict which sequences qualify.

column2: How complicated can the loop symmetries of a special space be?
column3: For special compact Kähler spaces, the claim says the fundamental group has an abelian subgroup of finite index: after passing to a finite cover, loop symmetries commute. Related claims cover specified orbifolds. For the noncompact algebraic setting, the conclusion concerns linear representations and allows a weaker, two-step nilpotent structure.

column2: Which projective spaces have universal covers of a simple algebraic shape?
column3: The manuscript classifies the universal covers that are semialgebraic, meaning describable by finitely many polynomial equalities and inequalities. It claims they split into three specified factors. If the cover is quasi-projective, one factor disappears; a space covered by complex Euclidean space has a finite cover by an abelian variety.

column2: Must certain complex surfaces contain a spherical shell?
column3: A spherical shell is a neighborhood shaped like the ordinary three-sphere, embedded holomorphically in a complex surface with connected complement. The manuscript claims every minimal compact class-VII surface with positive second Betti number contains one. Those classification and topology conditions are central to the statement.

column2: How many independent positive directions can a Fano space have?
column3: Fano spaces have a positive anticanonical bundle. The claim bounds the number of independent divisor directions in terms of dimension and the smallest anticanonical degree of a rational curve. It also identifies every equality case: a product of projective spaces of the specified dimension.

column2: Do curve-counting invariants obey the predicted Virasoro relations?
column3: Geometry can assign numbers to families of curves inside an algebraic space, with marked points carrying extra information. The manuscript claims an entire system of relations among these numbers for smooth projective complete intersections, in every genus. It also describes how the relations pass to certain projective-bundle constructions.

column2: Can geometric boundaries be completed using uniformly bounded denominators?
column3: A complement adjusts a boundary so the associated canonical data satisfy a prescribed relation while retaining controlled singularities. The claims give such complements for specified Fano-type spaces and contractions. The uniform bounds depend on dimension, singularity tolerance and, in the stated version, the allowed rational coefficients.

column2: Does nonnegative tangent geometry force symmetry in dimension six?
column3: The manuscript studies six-dimensional smooth projective Fano spaces whose tangent bundles are nonnegative in the specified sense. It claims every such space is homogeneous under an algebraic group: its points are equivalent under that symmetry action. This is the six-dimensional case, not the conjecture in every dimension.

column2: Does smooth nonnegative curvature produce a nonzero section?
column3: A line bundle can have favorable curvature without an obvious global section. For the anticanonical bundle on a smooth projective complex space, the claim says a smooth metric with nonnegative curvature guarantees a nonzero section of some positive tensor power. It does not prescribe one exponent for all spaces.

column2: Can dual symmetry groups give equivalent quantum geometric descriptions?
column3: For a simple complex algebraic group and its Langlands dual, the manuscript claims an equivalence between categories of twisted differential-equation data on a curve. The result covers the unramified de Rham setting and irrational shifted levels, retaining the specified global forms and components. These qualifications delimit the correspondence.

column2: Can every planar domain be reshaped into one with circular holes?
column3: A conformal map preserves angles locally. The manuscript claims every domain on the Riemann sphere is conformally equivalent to one whose missing components are round disks or points. A separate rigidity claim needs a removable boundary; it says certain conformal equivalences must then be Möbius transformations.

column2: How small can a set containing a segment in every direction be?
column3: A Kakeya set contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction. The claim says such a set in four-dimensional space must have full Hausdorff dimension. A separate three-dimensional result bounds how strongly a function can concentrate along thin tubes; full dimension does not mean positive volume.

column2: Can a polynomial with only plus-one and minus-one coefficients stay nearly flat?
column3: Move around the unit circle and measure the size of a polynomial’s value. The manuscript claims that, for every sufficiently large length, coefficients can be chosen so this size stays uniformly close to the square root of the length. It also claims unbounded merit factors for the resulting binary sequences.

column2: How much can waves from a curved surface reinforce each other?
column3: A Fourier extension operator combines oscillations whose frequencies lie on a surface. For every smooth compact positively curved surface in three dimensions, the claim bounds the resulting function using the same p-norm as the surface data whenever p exceeds three. It does not include the endpoint p equals three.

column2: How much smoothing makes a Fourier reconstruction bounded?
column3: Bochner–Riesz operators reconstruct functions while tapering frequencies near a cutoff. In three dimensions, the manuscript claims boundedness for every p in the stated range when the tapering strength is strictly above its specified threshold. The result concerns that strict range, not all boundary cases.

column2: Can a direction-dependent Hilbert transform stay bounded?
column3: Instead of integrating along one fixed direction, let the direction vary across the plane at a controlled rate. The claim bounds the resulting Hilbert transform in the squared-integral norm when integration stays within a sufficiently short scale. The scale depends on how quickly the direction field changes.

column2: Can a set fill almost an interval yet avoid every scaled geometric progression?
column3: Fix any ratio between zero and one. The manuscript constructs compact sets occupying arbitrarily close to the full length of an interval but containing no translated, nontrivially scaled copy of the infinite progression with that ratio. The set may depend on the ratio; finite progressions are a different question.

column2: Can a three-function singular integral be controlled by its inputs?
column3: This transform combines three functions sampled at offsets moving at different speeds, with cancellation around a singularity. The manuscript claims the total absolute size of the output is bounded by the product of the inputs’ cubic-integral norms for slopes one, two and three. It covers this particular exponent case.

column2: Which convex shapes minimize the volume product with their polar?
column3: A convex body has a partner called its polar, defined by linear inequalities. The manuscript claims the smallest possible product of their volumes is attained by the specified Hanner polytopes in the symmetric case and by simplices without symmetry, with all equality cases classified. Related claims concern functions and symplectic width.

column2: Can graph distances be represented by sums of coordinate differences?
column3: The L1 distance between two coordinate lists adds their absolute differences. The claim embeds shortest-path distances of planar graphs into such a space with bounded distortion, independent of graph size. For graphs of bounded treewidth, the bound depends only on treewidth. Related network flow–cut gaps are also bounded.

column2: How does volume behave when symmetric convex shapes are interpolated?
column3: The manuscript claims the logarithmic Brunn–Minkowski inequality, which controls volume under a specified interpolation of origin-symmetric convex bodies. It also gives concavity results for scaling under even log-concave measures. Symmetry and convexity are essential; the statement does not describe arbitrary shapes or arbitrary probability distributions.

column2: How much overlap is unavoidable when copies of a shape cover space?
column3: Cover all of n-dimensional space by translated copies of one convex body. The claim gives a covering density of at most a constant times n log n, even with translations restricted to a lattice. Some symmetric bodies need that much overlap up to constants, even without a lattice restriction.

column2: Can one-dimensional tail bounds control a whole probability distribution?
column3: For the centered log-concave distributions studied here, every linear measurement has a uniformly controlled, Gaussian-like tail. The manuscript claims this guarantees a logarithmic Sobolev inequality with a constant independent of dimension. The bound depends instead on the strength of those one-dimensional tail estimates.

column2: Can a finite distance pattern be compressed into far fewer coordinates?
column3: Take n points in an Lp space and allow any fixed distortion greater than one. The claim embeds them into a finite-dimensional space with the same p-distance using fewer than every fixed positive power of n coordinates asymptotically. Preserving distances exactly is much more expensive when p differs from two.

column2: Can plus and minus signs keep every running vector sum small?
column3: Given any finite list of vectors of length at most one in d dimensions, choose a sign for each. The manuscript claims every partial sum can be kept within a constant times the square root of d, regardless of list length. For zero-sum lists, it also gives a corresponding reordering result.

column2: Which convex shapes make the isotropic constant largest?
column3: The isotropic constant measures a normalized aspect of how a convex body’s mass is distributed. The manuscript claims simplices are its unique maximizers in every dimension. A related result identifies the smallest entropy allowed for log-concave densities and characterizes the distributions reaching equality.

column2: Can multiplying large matrices take fewer arithmetic operations?
column3: The manuscript claims new operation-count bounds for matrix multiplication. Over the complex numbers, square matrices can be multiplied using a count arbitrarily close to an n-to-the-nine-fourths power bound. Other bounds depend on the underlying field and matrix shape. These are arithmetic-operation claims, not measured software speedups.

column2: How large must a determinant representation of the permanent be?
column3: The permanent resembles a determinant but omits its alternating signs. The manuscript claims representing an n-by-n permanent by a determinant of affine-linear entries needs matrix size at least a constant times n cubed over the complex numbers. Allowing coefficientwise limiting representations does not evade the bound.

column2: How well can servers respond to requests without knowing what comes next?
column3: Move k servers through a distance space to serve requests as they arrive. The claim gives a randomized policy whose expected movement is within a squared-logarithmic competitive factor of the offline optimum, plus the allowed additive constant. Requests must be oblivious to the algorithm’s random choices.

column2: Can we efficiently estimate how many perfect matchings a graph has?
column3: A perfect matching pairs up every vertex using graph edges, with no vertex used twice. The manuscript claims a randomized approximation scheme for counting these pairings in arbitrary finite simple graphs, including exact recognition of a zero count. It estimates the number; it does not claim efficient exact counting.

column2: Can we count integer choices satisfying two sets of combinatorial rules?
column3: Polymatroids describe allowable allocations through rank constraints. The manuscript claims an efficient randomized estimate of how many integer bases satisfy two such systems simultaneously, given exact rank-query access. Each integer vector counts once. Related claims cover common independent sets of matroids under the specified oracle model.

column2: Can tables with fixed totals be sampled and counted efficiently?
column3: Imagine a nonnegative whole-number table whose row and column totals are prescribed. The claims provide exact uniform sampling in expected polynomial time and near-uniform sampling with a worst-case bound. A separate randomized counting approximation allows individual cell limits, including cells forced to zero.

column2: Can a short list of matrix substitutions detect a nonzero formula?
column3: When multiplication is noncommutative, changing the order of factors changes the answer. The manuscript constructs small matrix tests guaranteed to detect every nonzero division-free formula within a size bound over fields of a fixed characteristic. Rational formulas have an additional requirement: some rational-matrix evaluation must be defined.

column2: Which one-bit summary survives random noise best?
column3: Start with independent fair bits, summarize them by a Boolean function, and independently flip input bits with a fixed noise rate. The claim says keeping just one original coordinate maximizes mutual information in this setup. Stronger versions treat randomized summaries subject to specified information constraints.

column2: How many damaged copies are needed to reconstruct a binary string?
column3: Each observed copy has random bits deleted, hiding their original positions. At any fixed nonzero deletion rate below one, the manuscript claims some strings require more than polynomially many copies. It also gives quasipolynomial upper bounds in the stated setting, and polynomial bounds when deletion probability shrinks sufficiently fast.

column2: Can perfect matchings be described by a small semidefinite formulation?
column3: The perfect-matching polytope records all possible pairings of a graph’s vertices. The manuscript claims every exact description using a higher-dimensional positive-semidefinite lift requires exponential size. This rules out one compact representation strategy; it does not say finding a single perfect matching requires exponential time.

column2: How often can changing one bit flip a polynomial threshold decision?
column3: Evaluate a polynomial on a string of bits, then report only whether its value is nonnegative. The manuscript claims the average number of individual bits that can change that decision is at most eight times the polynomial’s degree times the square root of the number of bits.

column2: Can groups of bits influence a function much more than single bits?
column3: Sensitivity counts individual bit flips that change a Boolean output; block sensitivity allows disjoint groups to flip together. The manuscript constructs functions where block sensitivity exceeds a fixed power greater than two of sensitivity. This refutes the proposed quadratic bound, not every polynomial relationship.

column2: How expensive is a particular graph-comparison procedure?
column3: Weisfeiler–Leman refinement compares graphs by repeatedly updating descriptions of vertex tuples. The manuscript claims strong deterministic time lower bounds for its equivalence problem in the specified computation models. When tuple dimension is part of the input, certain versions are EXPTIME-complete, even for graphs of small maximum degree.

column2: How deeply must repetition be nested in a generalized regular expression?
column3: A Kleene star means repeating a pattern any number of times. The claim says every regular language can be described with at most three nested stars if expressions may also use complement, union and concatenation. Allowing complement matters; this is not a claim about ordinary expressions without it.

column2: How large must a shallow arithmetic circuit be for iterated matrix multiplication?
column3: The manuscript studies just one entry of a long product of variable matrices. It claims a sharp superpolynomial size bound for computing that entry using homogeneous depth-five sum–product circuits in characteristic zero. The restriction to this circuit model is essential; ordinary matrix multiplication algorithms use different structures.

column2: Can an endpoint problem have short, error-tolerant local verification?
column3: End-of-Line asks for an endpoint in an implicitly described directed graph. The manuscript translates it into numerical constraints with only a near-linear increase in size. Any assignment meeting almost all constraints to the specified accuracy yields an endpoint, and such assignments exist. This is a verification reduction, not a fast endpoint solver.

column2: Can we predict a machine’s bounded-time outcome using much less memory?
column3: For the specified one-writable-tape machines, the manuscript claims a simulation using roughly T to the two-fifths power in space, with logarithmic factors, to determine the outcome by time T. Its running time is unrestricted. The time cutoff matters: this does not decide whether a machine will ever halt.

column2: How many function queries are needed to sample a well-behaved distribution?
column3: For the strongly convex potentials specified here, the claim achieves fixed sampling accuracy with fewer than every fixed positive power of dimension in value-and-gradient queries. A minimizer is supplied, and computation between queries is unrestricted. A low query count therefore does not establish a comparably fast practical sampler.

column2: How does limited memory affect learning a direction?
column3: The manuscript considers a one-pass learner trying to recover a unit vector from noiseless Gaussian samples. With only a constant times dimension squared persistent bits, it claims a sample lower bound that grows with both dimension and requested accuracy. The final output may use only the stated terminal information.

column2: How hard is deciding whether real polynomial constraints have a solution?
column3: The manuscript places the existential theory of real numbers within the counting hierarchy, a family of complexity classes based on counting computation paths. A broader result handles one block of existential and one block of universal quantifiers. This gives a complexity upper bound, not a claim of polynomial-time solvability.

column2: Can a fixed-degree planar polynomial system have arbitrarily many isolated cycles?
column3: A limit cycle is an isolated closed orbit of a dynamical system. The claim says planar polynomial vector fields of any fixed degree have a finite uniform bound on their number. The bound may depend on degree. For classical quintic Liénard systems, the manuscript gives an exact maximum of two.

column2: Can one observable generate every mean-zero signal under a smooth motion?
column3: The manuscript constructs a smooth volume-preserving motion on a three-dimensional torus. It claims that repeatedly shifting one real observable forward and backward produces an orthonormal basis for all square-integrable mean-zero observables. This is the specific simple-spectrum behavior sought, not a description of every smooth chaotic system.

column2: Does ordinary mixing imply mixing among any finite number of events?
column3: Mixing means that two events become asymptotically independent when separated far enough in time. The manuscript claims that, for invertible probability-preserving transformations, this already forces the analogous behavior for every finite collection of events. All pairwise time separations must tend to infinity.

column2: Does the standard sine map have sustained chaos at large parameters?
column3: The standard sine map repeatedly moves points around a two-dimensional torus. The claim says that, for every sufficiently large positive parameter, its metric entropy with respect to area is positive. This measures dynamical complexity across the area distribution, rather than merely exhibiting a single unstable trajectory.

column2: Does a complete family of near-boundary billiard paths force an ellipse?
column3: Consider a smooth strictly convex billiard table. The claim says that if a whole grazing region is continuously filled by the specified invariant curves, the boundary must be an ellipse. This concerns a full near-boundary family, not just a few regular trajectories or isolated special paths.

column2: Can a self-similar measure’s dimension be read from entropy and contraction?
column3: Repeated random choices of shrinking maps create a self-similar measure on a line. The manuscript claims its dimension is determined by the entropy rate of the composed maps divided by the average contraction rate, capped at one. Exact overlaps and unequal contraction ratios are allowed in the stated formula.

column2: Will concentrations in certain reaction networks stay away from zero and infinity?
column3: For every finite weakly reversible mass-action system with fixed positive reaction rates, the claim gives an eventual common bounded region for positive trajectories in each compatibility class. Concentrations stay positively bounded below there. The bounds may depend on the class and system; this does not cover arbitrary reaction networks.

column2: Do billiards in every irrational-angle triangle weakly mix?
column3: The claim concerns the billiard flow on positions and directions in any nondegenerate triangle with at least one angle irrational relative to pi. It says this flow is weakly mixing under the specified natural measure. Weak mixing is a precise statistical property, not a claim that every individual path looks random.

column2: Can every abstract zero-entropy motion be realized by smooth geometry?
column3: The manuscript constructs an ergodic invertible probability-preserving transformation with zero entropy that cannot be represented by a smooth density-preserving diffeomorphism on any compact finite-dimensional manifold. One example rules out all finite dimensions. Thus zero entropy alone is not enough for this kind of smooth realization.

column2: Can every nine-dimensional set be divided into ten smaller-diameter pieces?
column3: Diameter measures the greatest separation between points of a set. The manuscript constructs a compact set in nine-dimensional space that cannot be covered by ten sets of strictly smaller diameter. It uses rank-one projection matrices to build the example, refuting the proposed universal covering rule in dimension nine.

column2: How long can a coloring avoid a one-color arithmetic progression?
column3: Color consecutive integers using a fixed number of colors. Eventually a long enough interval forces an equally spaced progression of a chosen length in one color. The claim says the necessary interval length grows faster than any fixed exponential in the progression length, with the stated uniform lower bound across color counts.

column2: Can sums and products of one finite set all share a color?
column3: Color the positive integers with finitely many colors. The manuscript claims there are sets of any prescribed finite size whose nonempty subset sums and nonempty subset products all have one common color. The claim is about arbitrarily large finite sets, not a single infinite set with this property.

column2: What is the minimum number of crossings in drawings of complete graphs?
column3: Draw every required edge in the plane and count crossings. The manuscript claims the classical formulas give the exact minimum for every complete graph and every complete bipartite graph. Curved continuous edges are allowed, so the result is not restricted to straight-line drawings.

column2: Does an order diagram determine a Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial?
column3: A Bruhat interval records which elements lie between two elements in a Coxeter group’s order. The claim says this abstract ordering alone determines the associated equal-parameter Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomial. Two matching intervals give the same polynomial even if they come from different Coxeter systems.

column2: Why are certain graph-coloring coefficients nonnegative?
column3: A chromatic quasisymmetric function packages information about graph colorings. For natural unit interval graphs, the manuscript claims its coefficients in the elementary basis are polynomials with nonnegative integer coefficients. It explains those coefficients by counting specified permutations, providing a combinatorial meaning for their positivity.

column2: How close are two estimates of when a random structure appears?
column3: Integral and fractional expectation thresholds are two ways to estimate the onset of a random property. The claim says they differ by at most a universal factor. A graph application decomposes edges into a bounded number of easier pieces, but their embeddings need not agree at shared vertices.

column2: Can expected subgraph counts predict when a graph appears randomly?
column3: Increase the edge probability of a random graph until a target graph usually appears. The manuscript claims this threshold is bounded by a universal constant times a logarithmic factor times the expectation threshold. The expectation test checks every subgraph of the target, rather than only the target’s own expected count.

column2: Do sparse higher-dimensional expanders exist in every dimension?
column3: Expander graphs connect very effectively without giving each vertex many neighbors. The manuscript claims analogous finite simplicial complexes exist in every dimension, with bounded vertex degrees and uniform coboundary expansion over the two-element field in all lower degrees. These are specific higher-dimensional expansion guarantees, not just visually dense connections.

column2: How long can an exceptionally low-correlation binary sequence be?
column3: A Barker sequence has only tiny correlations with its nontrivial shifts. Using the claimed classification of circulant real Hadamard matrices, the manuscript limits Barker sequences longer than one to seven listed lengths, ending at thirteen. The matrix claim allows only orders one and four.

column2: Can these planar graphs always be toured without revisiting a vertex?
column3: A Hamiltonian cycle visits every vertex exactly once before returning to its start. The manuscript claims one exists in every finite simple planar bipartite graph that has degree three at each vertex and remains connected after deleting any two vertices. Each of those structural assumptions restricts the claim.

column2: Can a dense graph be broken into only linearly many cycles and edges?
column3: Partition all edges of a finite simple graph into simple cycles and leftover single edges. The claim says a constant times the number of vertices always suffices, even if the original graph has far more edges. It bounds the number of pieces, not their lengths.

column2: How large can a set be if its differences avoid polynomial values?
column3: Choose integers from a long interval while forbidding nonzero differences equal to values of a fixed polynomial. Under the stated root-modulo-every-modulus condition, the claim bounds the set’s size by a power smaller than the interval length. A prime-input version requires the stronger unit-root condition.

column2: How many ways can a line separate part of a planar point set?
column3: Place points in the plane with no three on one line. The manuscript improves the upper bound on halving lines and, more generally, on subsets of a given size that a line can strictly separate. The improvement is by an absolute positive power, whose value is not made explicit.

column2: Does forbidding a fixed subgraph make coloring substantially easier?
column3: For graphs avoiding a fixed subgraph, the claim reduces the needed number of colors relative to maximum degree by a logarithmic factor, in the stronger correspondence-coloring setting. A companion gives large independent sets in graphs excluding a fixed clique. The constants depend on the forbidden graph or clique size.

column2: How sharply do random graph properties switch from unlikely to likely?
column3: As random edge probability increases, an increasing graph property changes from rare to common. The manuscript bounds how narrow this transition must be for properties unchanged by relabeling vertices. It gives related bounds for fixed-uniformity hypergraphs. The symmetry and monotonicity assumptions matter for the threshold claims.

column2: Can the first player force the Snaky shape on an infinite board?
column3: Two players alternate claiming empty squares. The manuscript claims the first player can guarantee the six-square Snaky pattern within twenty-one of their own moves, whatever the opponent does. Translations, rotations and reflections all count as the same winning shape under these rules.

column2: Must an algebraic intersection count be positive when dimensions fit?
column3: Serre’s intersection multiplicity is an algebraic way to count an intersection, allowing cancellations in its definition. The claim says the final count is strictly positive for the specified nonzero modules over a regular local ring when their intersection has finite length and their dimensions add to the ring’s dimension.

column2: Can multiplicity decrease under a flat local map?
column3: Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity measures a local ring’s algebraic thickness. The manuscript claims this number cannot decrease under a flat local homomorphism between the stated Noetherian local rings. Flatness is the condition controlling how algebraic relations behave during the change of rings; arbitrary ring maps are not covered.

column2: Can a complicated ideal be compared with a specially ordered monomial ideal?
column3: The manuscript claims that certain homogeneous ideals can be replaced by lex-plus-powers ideals while preserving their Hilbert function, which counts graded dimensions. The replacement has no smaller graded Betti numbers, measuring relations and higher relations. The claim assumes characteristic zero and a contained regular sequence of the stated degrees.

column2: Can two counts in finite-group representation theory be matched block by block?
column3: Representations describe group elements as linear transformations. In positive characteristic, their building blocks are organized into blocks. The manuscript claims the number of irreducible Brauer characters in each block equals the number of conjugacy classes of its weights, for every finite group and prime.

column2: Are there only finitely many block types with bounded defect?
column3: A defect group measures part of a representation block’s complexity in characteristic p. The claim says bounding its order leaves only finitely many block types up to Morita equivalence over each fixed algebraically closed field. A companion treats the specified integral coefficient rings; the equivalence is not literal equality.

column2: Does an invariant appearing after scaling already exist before scaling?
column3: Representations of the groups Spin(2n) are labeled by weights. The manuscript claims that, for three weights satisfying the stated root-lattice condition, an invariant appearing after any common positive integral scaling must already appear at the original weights. It is the type-D case of saturation.

column2: Can squaring one representation contain every irreducible representation?
column3: A tensor square combines a representation with itself. The claim says the square of each staircase representation contains every irreducible complex representation of its symmetric group. More generally, such an all-containing square exists for every symmetric-group size except the three specified exceptions: two, four and nine.

column2: Can trace information rule out unexpected idempotents in group algebras?
column3: An idempotent is an element unchanged by squaring. The manuscript constrains traces of idempotent matrices in a completed group algebra to finitely many finite-order conjugacy classes. An algebraic companion claims that torsion-free groups have no nontrivial idempotents over the specified characteristic-zero coefficient domains.

column2: Can every finite symmetric tensor category be faithfully modeled by a Verlinde category?
column3: A tensor category describes objects that can be combined, together with compatible maps between them. In positive characteristic, the manuscript claims each finite symmetric tensor category has a faithful, structure-preserving functor into a suitable higher Verlinde category. The required level can vary with the original category.

column2: Does changing the order of symmetric-power operations produce an inclusion?
column3: Taking a symmetric power combines vectors while ignoring their order. The manuscript claims the sixth symmetric power of a b-th symmetric power embeds into the reverse construction when b is at least six. It also gives a quadratic stabilization bound for a related map; it does not settle every case of Foulkes’ conjecture.

column2: Can a random fastest path extend optimally forever in both directions?
column3: Assign independent random travel times to edges of the planar grid. Under the stated continuity and moment assumptions, the claim rules out a path that remains fastest between any two of its points while extending infinitely both ways. Other results describe smoothness and strict convexity of limiting travel shapes for specified distributions.

column2: Does an infinite cluster already exist exactly at the percolation threshold?
column3: Randomly keep graph edges with probability p. On the infinite, locally finite, quasi-transitive graphs covered, the manuscript claims there is almost surely no infinite connected cluster at the critical probability when that probability is below one. The family also covers nearest-neighbor bond and site percolation on the three-dimensional grid.

column2: Can many infinite percolation clusters coexist before one becomes unique?
column3: On the specified nonamenable quasi-transitive graphs, the manuscript claims the threshold for having infinite clusters is strictly below the threshold for having just one. That leaves a genuine interval of edge probabilities with infinitely many infinite clusters. The graph assumptions distinguish this from ordinary Euclidean-lattice behavior.

column2: Does a two-dimensional spin model have the predicted continuum behavior?
column3: Neighboring spins interact on a lattice. The family claims exponential decay of spin correlations at every positive temperature for the stated O(n) models with n at least three. For O(3), it constructs a continuum theory with a positive mass gap; the O(4) result gives a precise gap asymptotic.

column2: Do small changes to the Ising model preserve its critical large-scale behavior?
column3: The manuscript claims that certain sufficiently weak, symmetry-preserving extra interactions leave the critical spin and energy limits unchanged. Under the stated conditions, interfaces have the same limiting random-curve law too. A disorder result also requires weak bounded independent randomness; arbitrary perturbations are not covered.

column2: If a walk escapes in one direction, must it make steady progress?
column3: A random walk moves through a random environment that assigns local transition probabilities. The claims give zero-or-one directional escape laws under the stated assumptions. In an independent uniformly elliptic environment, almost-sure directional escape additionally implies a deterministic limiting velocity with a positive component in that direction.

column2: Can a hierarchy of trial models give the exact free energy of a diluted spin glass?
column3: A diluted spin glass has random interactions among only some groups of spins. For the even-arity models satisfying the specified assumptions, the manuscript claims the limiting free energy equals an infimum over finite-depth hierarchical trial laws. The formula applies to that class, not every disordered spin model.

column2: What random curves describe critical cluster boundaries at large scales?
column3: The manuscript claims that interfaces of critical square-lattice random-cluster models converge to specified SLE random curves for the stated parameter range. It also gives a limiting law for complete nested loops when q is at least one. Domain regularity and boundary-approximation conditions vary across the parameter range.

column2: Do different percolation models share the same crossing laws near criticality?
column3: Poisson–Voronoi percolation colors cells in a random tessellation. The manuscript claims a precise critical crossing formula and, after each model’s own normalization, agreement of near-critical crossing thresholds with a triangular-lattice reference. The latter convergence is in probability over the random environment, not equality for each finite picture.

column2: How quickly does a spin glass forget its starting state?
column3: The manuscript studies single-spin heat-bath updates in the Gaussian Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model. It claims logarithmic-scale mixing at high temperature, a specified power-law scale at criticality, and stretched-exponential mixing from the stated Gibbs-sampled start at low temperature. The starting-state guarantee is different in those regimes.

column2: When can noisy descendants reveal their ancestor’s state?
column3: Send a label down a branching tree, adding noise at each step. For the specified three-state and four-state models, the claim gives the exact threshold for retaining information about the root, including failure at equality. The three-state result also yields a threshold for weak community recovery in a corresponding random graph model.

column2: How should the size of an SLE curve be measured exactly?
column3: SLE curves are random fractals, so ordinary length is not the right measure. The manuscript specifies a Hausdorff gauge, including a small logarithmic correction, that gives positive finite measure to each stated trace segment. Knowing the fractal dimension alone would not provide this exact measure normalization.

column2: Can a spanning forest be generated from independent labels without choosing a root?
column3: Give each vertex an independent random label. The manuscript claims one rule, respecting graph isomorphisms and requiring no root, can produce the free uniform spanning forest on every graph in the stated class. Related binary processes also admit such constructions. This does not assert that each output uses only a bounded neighborhood.

column2: Can random-matrix spin glasses have an exact thermodynamic formula?
column3: The interaction matrix is formed by randomly rotating a deterministic list of eigenvalues. Under the stated convergence and spectral-edge conditions, the claim gives an exact variational formula for the limiting pressure at every fixed temperature. Taking temperature toward zero then yields the zero-field ground-state energy.

column2: Is there a definite limiting threshold for random satisfiability?
column3: Add random k-SAT clauses to Boolean variables. For each fixed k of at least three, the manuscript claims a positive finite limiting transition threshold, together with a linear-order variance for the hitting time. It also claims computability of the 3-SAT threshold; that does not itself give a simple numerical formula.

column2: When can independent randomness generate the tree Ising state?
column3: On an infinite regular tree, the claim gives the exact temperature condition under which the free zero-field ferromagnetic Ising state can be constructed from independent vertex labels. The construction chooses no root and respects the stated symmetries. The threshold includes its boundary case and depends on the tree’s degree.

column2: How wide is a long self-avoiding walk?
column3: Choose uniformly among n-step walks on the honeycomb lattice that never revisit a vertex. The manuscript claims their diameter scales like n to the three-quarter power, up to smaller-order exponents. It also gives local mass and covering estimates, with high probability at each sufficiently large fixed length.

column2: Does uniqueness at one very large size force uniqueness at every larger size?
column3: A class of mathematical structures is categorical at a size if all its structures of that size are isomorphic. The manuscript claims a uniform sufficiently large threshold for abstract elementary classes beyond which categoricity at one size persists throughout the tail. A proposed particular threshold can still fail under the stated additional assumption.

column2: Can relative computability be relabeled without changing its order?
column3: Turing degrees group problems by what they can compute from each other, and order those degrees by relative computability. The claim says every order-preserving relabeling that is an automorphism fixes every degree. In that precise sense, the entire ordered structure has no nontrivial symmetries.

column2: Does every surjective image fitting back into its source imply choice?
column3: The manuscript claims, assuming set theory without choice is consistent, a model where every surjective image injects into its source but the axiom of choice still fails. Choice for ordinal-indexed families remains true there. This is a relative-consistency separation between principles, not a contradiction within ordinary choice-based set theory.

column2: If every typed expression can terminate, must every reduction path terminate?
column3: Weak normalization means each legal expression has some route to a normal form; strong normalization means every reduction route terminates. The manuscript claims the former property implies the latter for every pure type system in the stated setting. The assumption concerns all legal expressions, not just one expression with a lucky terminating path.

column2: Does a spherical boundary force a hyperbolic group to act on three-dimensional hyperbolic space?
column3: A word-hyperbolic group has a boundary describing directions toward infinity. When that boundary is a two-sphere, the claim gives a proper cocompact isometric action on hyperbolic three-space with finite kernel. If the group is torsion-free, it becomes the fundamental group of a closed hyperbolic three-manifold.

column2: Can finitely many generators and relations describe an infinite group of finite-order elements?
column3: The manuscript constructs an infinite finitely presented residually finite group in which every element has finite order equal to a power of two. Finite order for each element therefore does not force the group itself to be finite, even with these extra properties. Companion examples establish analogous failures in associative algebras.

column2: Can Thompson’s group F admit an invariant averaging rule?
column3: Thompson’s group F consists of specially constrained piecewise-linear transformations of an interval. Amenability asks whether the group admits a consistent invariant way of averaging bounded functions. The manuscript claims this group is nonamenable: no such averaging rule exists. The statement concerns this particular group, not all interval transformations.

column2: When can a group be embedded in a finitely presented simple group?
column3: The word problem asks whether a string of generators represents the identity. The manuscript claims a finitely generated group has a decidable word problem exactly when it embeds in some finitely presented simple group. The equivalence concerns existence of an algorithm, not a uniform efficient running time.

column2: Does turning bounded representations into unitary ones characterize amenability?
column3: A uniformly bounded representation describes group elements by linear operators whose sizes stay bounded. The manuscript claims all such Hilbert-space representations can be changed into unitary ones exactly for amenable discrete groups. For countable groups, it also gives an equivalence using stability of approximate unitary representations.

column2: Can every hyperbolic group be distinguished using finite quotients?
column3: Residual finiteness means each nonidentity element remains nontrivial in some finite quotient. The manuscript constructs a torsion-free word-hyperbolic group failing this property. In fact, one fixed nonidentity element disappears under every finite-dimensional representation over every field, ruling out faithful linear representations as well.

column2: Can an infinite simple finitely presented group still be amenable?
column3: Simple groups have no proper nontrivial normal subgroups; finitely presented groups use finitely many generators and relations; amenable groups admit an invariant averaging rule. The manuscript constructs one infinite group with all three properties. The point is their coexistence, not a classification of all groups having them.

column2: Do Artin groups have the predicted classifying spaces and subgroup intersections?
column3: The manuscript claims the Salvetti complex for every finite-rank Artin group has no higher homotopy, making it the predicted classifying space. It also says arbitrary intersections of parabolic subgroups remain parabolic. A separate example shows that a desirable nonpositive-curvature action need not exist for every Artin group.

column2: Can large-scale geometry recognize virtually polycyclic groups?
column3: Quasi-isometry compares spaces while allowing bounded errors and fixed stretching factors, ignoring fine-scale details. The manuscript claims a finitely generated group looking this way like a virtually polycyclic group must itself be virtually polycyclic. It recognizes that structural class, not the exact original group.

column2: Does hyperbolic large-scale geometry always come from a CAT(0) action?
column3: CAT(0) spaces satisfy a metric form of nonpositive curvature. The manuscript constructs a word-hyperbolic group that cannot act properly and cocompactly by isometries on any proper complete CAT(0) space, in any dimension. Thus these two ways of describing negative or nonpositive geometry are not interchangeable.

column2: Which one-relator groups are word-hyperbolic?
column3: A one-relator group is described by generators subject to one relation. The claim says every finitely generated such group is word-hyperbolic when it contains none of the specified Baumslag–Solitar subgroups. It also claims every hyperbolic one-relator group has a finite-index subgroup that is compact special.

column2: Can different actions of the same group have different costs?
column3: Cost measures the amount of generating structure needed to describe the orbit relation of a probability-preserving action. The manuscript constructs one finitely generated group with two essentially free actions of different costs. This disproves fixed price in general; cost is a mathematical invariant, not computational runtime or money.

column2: Does the area surrounding a trapped region bound a spacetime’s mass?
column3: Under the stated energy, trapping and decay assumptions, the manuscript claims a sharp lower bound on total invariant mass in terms of minimum enclosing area for asymptotically flat initial data. It covers all spatial dimensions at least three. Equality and charged versions require their additional hypotheses.

column2: How does dimension change localization in a random lattice potential?
column3: The Anderson model describes an operator on a lattice with random site potentials. For independent uniform potentials, the claim gives pure-point spectrum in two dimensions at every positive disorder strength. In dimensions at least three, sufficiently weak disorder instead gives absolutely continuous spectrum on a specified open energy interval.

column2: What is the sharp bound on negative quantum energy levels in one dimension?
column3: Lieb–Thirring inequalities compare negative eigenvalues of a Schrödinger operator with an integral of its potential. For the stated exponent range, the manuscript claims the sharp scalar constant also works for arbitrary finite matrix-valued potentials. It characterizes every equality case using specified scalar soliton profiles and zero channels.

column2: How many electrons can a molecule bind beyond its nuclear charge?
column3: In the stated nonrelativistic Coulomb model, the manuscript claims a molecule binds at most its total nuclear charge plus a universal constant times its number of nuclei. It also bounds neutral-atom ionization energies and specified outer radii, and gives asymptotic statements under particular large-charge limits.

column2: Are generic small perturbations of a Kerr bridge inextendible?
column3: The manuscript studies vacuum initial data near a fixed rotating subextremal Kerr bridge. It claims a dense generic set develops spacetimes that cannot be extended with the specified weak regularity. This is a local generic result with precise extension conditions, not a statement about every conceivable black-hole spacetime.

column2: Does a uniform energy gap bound entanglement by boundary size in two dimensions?
column3: For unique ground states of the stated finite-range square-lattice systems, the manuscript claims an entanglement area law from a uniform spectral gap and local interaction bounds. On open squares it also supplies tensor-network approximations with polynomial bond dimension and a specified global error, under the stronger stated setup.

column2: How many mutually unbiased bases can six-dimensional complex space contain?
column3: Two orthonormal bases are mutually unbiased when every vector from one has equal-sized overlap with every vector from the other. The manuscript claims dimension six allows three such bases but not four. The exclusion relies on a certified computation with specified arithmetic and compiler conditions, which remain part of its scope.

column2: Does the spin-one antiferromagnetic chain retain an energy gap as it grows?
column3: The claim says the gap between the ground state and excited energies stays bounded away from zero for the pure spin-one Heisenberg model on even periodic rings. A companion treats odd open chains with a particular endpoint field. Boundary conditions differ between the two results and are not interchangeable.

column2: Is the Laughlin state separated from excitations even with weak disorder?
column3: For the specified one-third-filled fermionic model on a round sphere, the manuscript claims a uniform positive gap above its unique ground state. That gap survives sufficiently weak bounded scalar one-body potentials after projection to the lowest Landau level. The model, geometry and permitted perturbations are part of the claim.

column2: How many bound zero-energy states does the BFSS matrix model have?
column3: For each finite size at least two, the manuscript claims the relative SU(N) BFSS model has exactly one normalizable state of zero energy. For SU(2), a companion also claims infinitely many normalizable positive-energy eigenstates. Zero-energy uniqueness therefore does not mean uniqueness among all bound states.

column2: How does a quantum ferromagnet lose magnetization at very low temperature?
column3: The manuscript claims Bloch’s three-halves power law with its exact coefficient for the specified three-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnets. It also establishes spontaneous magnetization in the stated higher-dimensional nearest-neighbor models. The order of the infinite-volume, zero-field and low-temperature limits is essential to these statements.

column2: How much entropy remains when two independent quantum light inputs are mixed?
column3: A beam splitter combines two bosonic inputs with a chosen transmissivity. The claim gives a lower bound on the output’s entropy photon number, a quantity translating entropy into an equivalent thermal photon count. The inputs are independent of one another, though each may contain internal entanglement.

column2: Can a constant-depth quantum circuit reliably compute parity?
column3: Parity records whether a bit string has an odd number of ones. In the specified circuit model with polynomially many qubits, the manuscript claims constant depth cannot achieve any fixed positive worst-case advantage. The available gates, zero-initialized ancillas and single measured output are explicit restrictions on the claim.

column2: How much classical information can an amplitude-damping qubit channel transmit?
column3: This noisy quantum channel models damping with a thermal parameter. The manuscript claims its unassisted classical capacity for every parameter choice, expressed through a one-variable optimization. Independent two-state signal ensembles attain the capacity with collective decoding. The result concerns this channel family and does not assume additional shared assistance.

column2: Can entanglement defeat repetition as a way to suppress excess wins?
column3: Repeat a finite two-player one-round game independently many times. If the best entangled single-game winning probability is below one, the claim says exceeding that rate by a fixed positive amount becomes exponentially unlikely. Players may coordinate across repetitions using a joint finite-dimensional entangled strategy.

column2: Do algebraic and operator descriptions of certain conformal theories agree?
column3: The manuscript starts from a simple unitary strongly rational vertex operator algebra and claims it produces a completely rational conformal net. It also matches the corresponding representation categories. These are two precise mathematical encodings of conformal structure; the strong rationality and unitarity assumptions restrict the class covered.

column2: Can QAOA approach the optimal energy of a random spin glass?
column3: The claim says that for any requested energy accuracy, a finite QAOA depth and fixed angles suffice in the stated Gaussian spin-glass limit. System size goes to infinity before depth. This gives an asymptotic expected-energy guarantee, not exact finite-instance optimization or an efficient bound on depth versus accuracy.

column2: When does scale symmetry force local conformal symmetry?
column3: Scale symmetry concerns changing all lengths together; conformal symmetry allows a richer set of local angle-preserving changes. Under the listed spectral, current and reconstruction assumptions, the manuscript claims the implication in four-dimensional unitary theories. Its conclusion concerns local identities, not a global conformal action on the entire theory.

column2: How large can the query advantage of a quantum algorithm be?
column3: For total Boolean functions, randomized and quantum algorithms can require different numbers of input-bit queries. The manuscript claims the known fourth-power relationship is sharp: no smaller universal exponent works. Computation between queries is unrestricted, so this measures information access rather than total execution time.

column2: Do free groups with different generator counts produce different von Neumann factors?
column3: A free group factor is an operator algebra built from a free group. The manuscript claims the factors from two and three generators are isomorphic, and consequently all interpolated free group factors are isomorphic. The groups themselves remain different; it is their associated operator algebras that are identified.

column2: Can every bounded algebra representation be adjusted to preserve adjoints?
column3: A bounded representation of a C*-algebra need not initially respect the adjoint operation. The claim says changing coordinates by a bounded invertible operator always makes it a *-homomorphism under the stated unitality and complex-linearity assumptions. This preserves the algebraic representation while correcting its Hilbert-space compatibility.

column2: Can a simpler subalgebra retain the same commutation information?
column3: The bicentralizer problem concerns operators that asymptotically commute with specified families of other operators. The manuscript claims its predicted resolution for type III1 factors with separable predual. A relative version constructs an amenable subalgebra preserving the stated commutant in the continuous core, under a conditional-expectation assumption.

column2: Do three regularity properties of nuclear operator algebras coincide?
column3: The manuscript claims equivalence between strict comparison, finite nuclear dimension and absorbing the Jiang–Su algebra for the specified simple unital nuclear C*-algebras. It also makes Jiang–Su absorption compatible with amenable group actions in the stated stably finite setting. These are structural regularity results with substantial hypotheses.

column2: Can every separable operator algebra fit inside a nuclear norm ultrapower?
column3: An ultrapower combines infinitely many copies of one algebra through a limiting construction. The manuscript gives an explicit separable unital group C*-algebra that cannot embed unitally into the norm ultrapower of any fixed nonzero unital nuclear C*-algebra. The choice of norm ultrapower, rather than another completion, matters.

column2: Must an operator have a nontrivial subspace preserved by everything commuting with it?
column3: Such a subspace is called hyperinvariant. The manuscript constructs a nonzero operator on each infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space with no nontrivial closed hyperinvariant subspace, even though its spectral radius is zero. This does not say the operator has no ordinary invariant subspaces; that is a different condition.

column2: Do higher bounded Hochschild cohomology classes always vanish?
column3: Hochschild cohomology records whether algebraically compatible multilinear data come from simpler data one degree lower. The manuscript claims every bounded cocycle of degree at least two on a complex von Neumann algebra has a bounded primitive when coefficients lie in the algebra itself. It does not address arbitrary coefficient modules here.

column2: Can one operator generate an entire separable type II1 factor?
column3: Generating a von Neumann algebra allows algebraic operations, adjoints and the relevant operator limits. The manuscript claims one operator always suffices for a type II1 factor with separable predual, equivalently two self-adjoint operators. A stronger companion concerns adding one unitary to the specified irreducible subalgebra.

column2: Do two definitions of free entropy agree when both are finite?
column3: One definition uses approximating matrices; another uses free Fisher information. The manuscript constructs a bounded self-adjoint tuple for which both entropy values are finite but strictly different. The example therefore separates the definitions without relying on an infinite or undefined value to create the discrepancy.

column2: Can central sequences detect Jiang–Su stability?
column3: Central sequences approximately commute with each fixed element of an algebra. The manuscript claims that, for the specified unital separable C*-algebras, absence of one-dimensional representations of their norm central-sequence algebra exactly characterizes Jiang–Su absorption. A companion gives absorption for infinite tensor powers when the original algebra has no characters.

column2: How many blocks are needed to pave a self-adjoint operator?
column3: Paving breaks an operator into diagonal blocks relative to a maximal commuting subalgebra so each block has controlled norm. The claim gives a block count proportional to the inverse square of the error tolerance. Its strong-operator version allows a compression approaching the identity; this qualification distinguishes it from unrestricted norm paving.

column2: Can a dynamical system’s mean dimension determine an operator-algebra invariant?
column3: A minimal homeomorphism yields a crossed-product C*-algebra. The manuscript claims its radius of comparison is exactly half the system’s mean dimension, including infinite values. In the zero-mean-dimension case, it also identifies equivalent regularity properties and bounds nuclear dimension by one. The system must satisfy the stated minimality and compactness conditions.

column2: Does ordinary pure infiniteness imply its stronger operator-algebra version?
column3: Pure infiniteness describes a form of abundant internal duplication in a C*-algebra. The manuscript claims the ordinary and strong versions coincide. For the specified exact and nuclear algebras, further criteria imply absorption of the infinite Cuntz algebra. These structural meanings of “infinite” are more specific than simply having infinitely many elements.

column2: Must a locally compact group acting faithfully on a manifold be a Lie group?
column3: A Lie group has a smooth, finite-dimensional group structure. The manuscript claims any locally compact second-countable group acting faithfully and continuously on the stated connected finite-dimensional topological manifold must have that structure. Faithfulness means distinct group elements act differently; the theorem includes the listed topological assumptions.

column2: Do algebraic intersection conditions guarantee disjoint disks in four dimensions?
column3: The manuscript gives a negative answer: the specified framed dual spheres do not always allow disjoint locally flat spanning disks. It also constructs a four-dimensional Poincaré duality group that cannot be the fundamental group of a closed aspherical topological four-manifold. Algebraic resemblance alone therefore does not ensure the desired geometric realization.

column2: Can different surgeries on a nontrivial knot give the same oriented manifold?
column3: Dehn surgery removes a knot neighborhood and glues it back with a chosen slope. The claim says two distinct slopes on a nontrivial smooth knot in the three-sphere never yield manifolds related by an orientation-preserving homeomorphism. Preserving orientation is part of the statement, including when one slope is meridional.

column2: Can a coarse assembly map lose nontrivial rational information?
column3: Coarse assembly relates large-scale geometric data to operator-algebraic data. The manuscript builds a separated union of finite bounded-degree graphs for which a nontrivial infinite-order class maps to zero. It gives this failure for both maximal and reduced versions, refuting the stated rational injectivity expectation.

column2: Do finite Smith–Toda spectra exist at every height if the prime can change?
column3: These spectra are finite objects in stable homotopy theory with a specifically prescribed homology pattern. The manuscript claims one can be constructed at every height, choosing a suitable prime for that height. It does not assert existence at every fixed prime; an explicit height-four example uses prime 1009.

column2: Which prime-three Kervaire classes survive the homotopy calculation?
column3: A spectral sequence is a staged calculation in which candidate classes may disappear along the way. The manuscript claims exactly three of the specified standard prime-three Kervaire candidates survive, at indices zero, two and three. Each surviving detection class contains an element of exact additive order three.

column2: Does the arrangement of elementary abelian subgroups have nontrivial topology?
column3: Arrange a finite group’s nontrivial elementary abelian p-subgroups by inclusion. If the largest normal p-subgroup is trivial, the manuscript claims this arrangement has nonzero reduced rational homology. It therefore cannot be contracted to a point. This is the rational-homology version of Quillen’s conjecture.

column2: How many tensor-closed classes occur at a fixed chromatic height?
column3: Stable homotopy theory organizes information by a prime and a height. Using a claimed result on invariant ideals of deformation rings, the manuscript identifies exactly n plus two thick tensor ideals among dualizable height-n local spectra. It also describes their associated spectrum as a chain of n plus one points.

column2: Can algebraic higher groupoids reproduce the homotopy theory of spaces?
