column3: Homotopy studies spaces up to continuous deformation. An infinity-groupoid records objects, reversible paths, paths between paths, and higher levels of such data algebraically. The manuscript claims these objects recover the homotopy theory of spaces for every Grothendieck coherator in the specified convention. The chosen definition is part of the result.

column2: Is each homotopy group of the local sphere finitely generated?
column3: After isolating a prime and chromatic height, the local sphere has a homotopy group in each degree. The manuscript claims each can be generated by finitely many elements over the p-adic integers. Finitely generated does not necessarily mean finite as a set, and the assertion is made degree by degree.

column2: How much chromatic information can be lost when taking fixed points?
column3: Taking points fixed by a larger subgroup can lower the chromatic height detected in an equivariant spectrum. For finite p-groups, the manuscript claims the worst possible loss equals the shortest specified subgroup-chain length with cyclic quotients. Each quotient counts once, regardless of its size, and examples attain the bound.

column2: Where can square-integrable topology survive in an aspherical four-manifold’s cover?
column3: An aspherical space has a contractible universal cover, but its L2-Betti numbers measure a different, size-normalized kind of topology. The manuscript claims these numbers vanish outside the middle degree for closed aspherical topological four-manifolds. It extends the assertion to the stated finite four-dimensional Poincaré complexes.

column2: Which stable homotopy classes remain visible in mod-two homology?
column3: The Hurewicz map sends homotopy information to homology, which can forget much of it. The manuscript claims the positive-degree image for the sphere is generated only by the specified Hopf-invariant-one and existing Kervaire-invariant-one classes. This limits the image of that map, not all stable homotopy classes themselves.

column2: Can strict higher categories model spaces up to homotopy?
column3: Higher categories have objects, maps, maps between maps, and further levels. The manuscript claims small strict globular categories admit suitable model structures equivalent to simplicial sets in every stated finite dimension and the infinite case. This concerns equivalence of homotopy theories, rather than literal equality of individual categories and spaces.

column2: Does the metric on a unit sphere determine the whole Banach space?
column3: The manuscript claims any distance-preserving bijection between the unit spheres of two nonzero real Banach spaces extends uniquely to a linear distance-preserving bijection of the whole spaces. Thus exact sphere distances determine the linear metric structure, even in infinite dimensions. The map must preserve distances exactly, not approximately.

column2: Do roughly matching distances determine a Banach space’s linear structure?
column3: The manuscript constructs two separable real Banach spaces with a bijection that stretches and shrinks distances by only bounded factors, but with no linear isomorphism between them. Thus bi-Lipschitz equivalence preserves less than linear structure. This differs from preserving every distance exactly, as in family 322.

column2: Can an operator polynomial’s norm be bounded using its numerical range?
column3: The numerical range collects the scalar values obtained by testing an operator against unit vectors. The manuscript claims the norm of a matrix-valued polynomial evaluated at that operator is at most twice its largest norm on this set. The factor two is optimal and independent of matrix size.

column2: Can random-sign behavior in a space and its dual force better geometry?
column3: Cotype measures how random signed sums reflect the sizes of their component vectors. The manuscript claims finite cotype for both a real Banach space and its dual forces K-convexity, provided the space has the approximation property. That extra approximation assumption is essential to the stated version.

column2: Can controlled random-walk behavior reveal a uniformly convex norm?
column3: Markov type bounds how distances accumulate along random walks mapped into a space. The claim says a real Banach space with any Markov type above one can be given an equivalent uniformly convex norm. Changing the norm preserves the linear topology, but need not preserve each original distance.

column2: Must a distance-nonincreasing map leave some point fixed?
column3: Take a nonempty closed bounded convex subset of a real reflexive Banach space. The manuscript claims every self-map that never increases distances fixes at least one point. It uses the original norm and does not require uniform convexity. The reflexivity and geometric restrictions on the subset delimit the result.

column2: Does good midpoint behavior force stronger asymptotic convexity?
column3: The manuscript constructs a reflexive Banach space whose norm has the specified asymptotic midpoint convexity but cannot be replaced by an equivalent asymptotically uniformly convex norm. Increasingly deep branching diamond graphs need increasing distortion to fit into it. The example separates two closely related notions of convexity.

column2: Can a distance-controlled map into ℓ1 be extended everywhere?
column3: The ℓ1 distance adds absolute coordinate differences. The manuscript claims any Lipschitz map from a subset of a real Hilbert space into ℓ1 extends to the entire space with at most one universal multiplicative increase in its Lipschitz constant. It derives this from a claimed metric Markov cotype property.

column2: Can every closed curved surface fit isometrically into four-dimensional Euclidean space?
column3: The manuscript claims any smooth closed Riemannian surface admits a smooth isometric immersion into four-dimensional Euclidean space. The map preserves its intrinsic metric, including for nonorientable surfaces. An immersion may overlap itself, so this does not promise a non-self-intersecting embedding or preservation of straight-line distances between distant points.

column2: Can every smooth surface metric be realized locally in three dimensions?
column3: The manuscript constructs a smooth metric on a planar patch that cannot be smoothly immersed isometrically into three-dimensional Euclidean space near the origin. Shrinking the neighborhood does not help. Thus some perfectly smooth intrinsic distance rules have no such local three-dimensional realization.

column2: Does topological complexity force a minimum amount of negative scalar curvature?
column3: The manuscript claims an integral lower bound on the negative part of scalar curvature in terms of simplicial volume, a topological invariant. Related claims restrict spaces admitting positive scalar curvature and force flatness for nonnegative-scalar-curvature metrics on closed aspherical manifolds. The different conclusions have their stated hypotheses.

column2: Can a curvature condition force a space to be thin in two directions?
column3: The manuscript claims a complete manifold satisfying the specified spectral scalar-curvature inequality maps continuously into a complex at least two dimensions lower, with uniformly bounded diameters of entire fibers. This is a precise large-scale width bound, not a claim that the original manifold actually has fewer local dimensions.

column2: How much boundary is needed to enclose a given volume in nonpositive curvature?
column3: For the stated complete simply connected manifolds, the manuscript claims the sharp boundary-size comparison with a ball in the constant-curvature model. In the zero-curvature equality case, the specified bounded regions must be Euclidean balls. Companion claims control fillings in the broader class of proper CAT(0) spaces.

column2: Does positive complex curvature force a space to be complex Euclidean space?
column3: The manuscript claims every complete connected noncompact Kähler manifold with strictly positive holomorphic bisectional curvature is biholomorphic to complex Euclidean space. Biholomorphic means equivalent through holomorphic coordinates; it does not mean the original curved metric is the flat Euclidean metric.

column2: When does the natural geodesic-flow measure maximize entropy?
column3: Geodesic flow follows straightest possible motion on a curved manifold. For closed negatively curved manifolds of dimension at least three, the claim says the natural normalized Liouville measure maximizes entropy exactly when the metric is locally symmetric. This connects a statistical property of motion with a rigid geometric condition.

column2: Can a positive triple of two-forms be deformed into hyperkähler geometry?
column3: The manuscript starts with three closed two-forms on a closed oriented four-manifold satisfying a positivity condition. After the stated normalization, it claims they can be deformed to a hyperkähler triple while retaining positivity and their cohomology classes throughout. This is a structured deformation claim, not an arbitrary change of metric.

column2: Can a taming symplectic form be replaced by a compatible one?
column3: On a closed four-manifold, an almost complex structure behaves locally like multiplication by the imaginary unit. If some symplectic form tames it, the claim says a form fully compatible with it exists. The almost complex structure stays fixed, but the new form need not keep the old cohomology class.

column2: When can several symplectic balls fit inside one larger ball?
column3: Symplectic embeddings preserve a geometric two-form, making packing stricter than merely fitting by volume. In dimensions six and higher, the manuscript claims exactly two conditions suffice: a strict total-volume inequality and a strict pairwise-capacity inequality. These concern closed balls inside an open ball with the stated capacities.

column2: Does equality of injectivity radius and diameter force a standard geometry?
column3: Injectivity radius measures how far geodesic coordinates remain unambiguous; diameter is the greatest distance between points. The manuscript claims that when these are equal on a closed connected Riemannian manifold, its metric must be a scaled standard compact rank-one symmetric metric. The equality is a strong restriction.

column2: Must spheres have infinitely many genuinely different closed geodesics?
column3: A closed geodesic is a loop that follows the metric’s straightest paths. The claim says every smooth Riemannian sphere of dimension at least two has infinitely many with distinct images, not just repeated laps of one loop. It extends to the stated spherical covers and all closed three-manifolds.

column2: How small can a non-equatorial minimal hypersurface in a round sphere be?
column3: Minimal hypersurfaces are stationary for volume under local variations. The manuscript claims any closed connected minimal immersion in the stated round sphere, excluding totally geodesic images, has volume at least that of the smallest minimal Clifford product. Volume counts covering multiplicity, so repeated coverings are not treated as one copy.

column2: How large can the zero set of a Laplace eigenfunction become?
column3: An eigenfunction’s nodal set is where it vanishes. On a fixed smooth closed surface, the manuscript claims its length is bounded by a constant times the square root of the eigenvalue. In dimensions three and four it constructs failures of the analogous upper bound, with stronger growth examples in dimension five.

column2: Can weak analytic curvature tests exactly characterize Alexandrov curvature?
column3: Alexandrov curvature bounds compare triangles in a metric space with triangles in model spaces. The manuscript claims these bounds are equivalent to the specified combination of an RCD condition and distributional sectional-curvature inequalities, with Hausdorff measure and full support. The measure choice and original global test classes remain part of the criterion.

column2: Does having no conjugate points imply some nonpositively curved metric exists?
column3: Conjugate points describe a particular way nearby geodesics can refocus. The manuscript constructs a closed orientable three-manifold with a metric having no conjugate points, yet with no metric of nonpositive sectional curvature at all. This separates existence of the two kinds of geometry on the same underlying manifold.

column2: Does negative Kähler curvature guarantee bounded holomorphic coordinates?
column3: The manuscript constructs a contractible domain in complex three-space carrying a complete negatively pinched Kähler metric but admitting no bounded holomorphic coordinate realization. A higher-dimensional example has only constant bounded holomorphic functions. The examples show that these negative-curvature conditions do not imply the proposed bounded-domain uniformization.

column2: Can the same gas density evolve into two different conserving solutions?
column3: For the three-dimensional periodic hard-sphere Boltzmann equation, the manuscript constructs two distinct global entropy solutions from the same initial density. Both retain the stated continuity and exact local conservation of mass, momentum and energy. The nonuniqueness concerns this solution class; the claim does not assert two smooth classical solutions.

column2: Can measurements on just one boundary patch reveal interior geometry?
column3: Under the stated smoothness and bundle assumptions, zero-frequency input and response on one nonempty open boundary patch determine the metric and connection up to allowed coordinate and gauge changes. A contrasting example with merely measurable conductivity shows full-boundary data need not give uniqueness at lower regularity.

column2: Can rough invertible three-dimensional maps be approximated by smooth invertible ones?
column3: A Sobolev homeomorphism is continuous and invertible but has derivatives understood in an integrated weak sense. The manuscript claims every such map between the stated bounded three-dimensional domains can be approximated strongly in the same finite-p Sobolev norm by smooth diffeomorphisms onto the same target. No claim is made for p equal to infinity.

column2: Where are the hot and cold spots of the first nonconstant Neumann mode?
column3: The manuscript studies the first positive Neumann eigenvalue on a smooth bounded planar domain with no holes. It claims every corresponding nonzero eigenfunction has no critical point in the interior, so its maximum and minimum lie on the boundary. This is not a claim about every possible temperature profile or eigenmode.

column2: When can two coupled nonlinear elliptic equations have positive solutions everywhere?
column3: The manuscript claims nonexistence of positive entire solutions to the stated weighted Lane–Emden system in its subcritical parameter range, without assuming symmetry or growth bounds. The solutions still must satisfy the listed regularity conditions. Combined with known radial examples, it yields an exact criterion only in the specified further range.

column2: Can a defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation still blow up?
column3: Defocusing does not prevent every kind of singular behavior in every dimension. The manuscript claims finite-time blowup for an open set of initial data on a twelve-dimensional torus with sufficiently high odd nonlinearity. The blowup persists under the stated Sobolev perturbations; it is not a claim about ordinary three-dimensional regimes.

column2: Can static boundary measurements identify an elastic material’s two coefficients?
column3: Prescribe displacements on the boundary and measure the resulting traction. The manuscript claims the complete static response determines both smooth Lamé coefficients inside a bounded three-dimensional domain, under the stated positivity conditions. It needs neither analyticity nor prior knowledge near the boundary, but it does use full boundary data.

column2: Must an optimal three-particle arrangement be determined by one particle’s position?
column3: For suitable smooth identical spatial densities, the manuscript claims the least Coulomb cost cannot be attained by making the other two positions deterministic functions of the first. Randomized couplings can attain the optimum, while deterministic ones only approach it. Similar examples cover the stated inverse-power costs.

column2: How much can an optimal transport map change when its target changes?
column3: The manuscript claims a cube-root stability bound for quadratic optimal transport from a uniform measure on a compact convex body to targets in a fixed compact set. The exponent is sharp, even for targets on three points. This rules out the proposed stronger square-root bound under these assumptions.

column2: Can a viscous fluid encode a universal computation?
column3: The manuscript constructs smooth externally forced incompressible flows whose designated particle reaches a fixed region exactly when an encoded machine halts. A finite program specifies the force, and viscosity is fixed and positive. This concerns carefully engineered forcing, not an unforced flow or a claim to decide the halting problem.
